m-proof:
Key ideas
  • Proof by deduction: start from known facts and use logical steps to reach the statement in general.
  • Proof by exhaustion: split into a finite set of cases and check every one (e.g. n even / n odd, or n \equiv 0,1,2 \pmod 3).
  • Disproof by counter-example: a single case where the statement fails is enough.
  • Proof by contradiction: assume the statement is false, then show this leads to something impossible.
Useful forms
  • Even: 2k; odd: 2k+1; consecutive integers: n,\ n+1; rational: \frac{a}{b} with a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, b \neq 0, no common factors.
  • Completing the square proves positivity: x^2-6x+10=(x-3)^2+1>0 for all real x.
Classic proofs
  • **\sqrt{2} is irrational:** assume \sqrt2=\frac ab in lowest terms. Then a^2=2b^2, so a is even, a=2c, giving b^2=2c^2, so b is even too, contradicting "lowest terms".
  • Infinitely many primes: assume finitely many, p_1,\dots,p_n. Then N=p_1p_2\cdots p_n+1 leaves remainder 1 when divided by every p_i. So N is prime or has a prime factor not in the list. Contradiction.
Worked example

Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.

n+(n+1)+(n+2)=3n+3=3(n+1)

3(n+1) is a multiple of 3, so the result holds for all integers n.

Exam tips

Write a concluding sentence that restates what has been proved, e.g. "…therefore it is divisible by 3".

  • In contradiction proofs, state clearly what you are assuming and where the contradiction is.
  • A list of examples is not a proof (unless it is exhaustion over *all* cases).
m-alg:
Indices and surds
  • a^m a^n=a^{m+n}, \ (a^m)^n=a^{mn}, \ a^{-n}=\frac1{a^n}, \ a^{\frac mn}=(\sqrt[n]a)^m.
  • Rationalise: \dfrac{1}{\sqrt a+\sqrt b}=\dfrac{\sqrt a-\sqrt b}{a-b}.
Quadratics
  • Discriminant b^2-4ac: >0 two real roots, =0 one repeated root, <0 no real roots.
  • Completed square a(x+p)^2+q gives the turning point (-p,\,q).
x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}
Inequalities
  • For a quadratic inequality, find the critical values and sketch. E.g. x^2-x-6<0 \Rightarrow -2<x<3.
  • Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
Polynomials
  • Factor theorem: f(a)=0 \iff (x-a) is a factor.
  • Algebraic division (or comparing coefficients) gives the other factor.
Functions
  • Composite fg(x)=f(g(x)): apply g first.
  • Inverse f^{-1}: swap x and y and rearrange. Its graph is the reflection of f in y=x. Domain of f^{-1} = range of f.
  • Modulus: solve |f(x)|=k using f(x)=\pm k, and check graphically.
  • Transformations: f(x)+a is up a; f(x+a) is left a; af(x) stretches vertically by factor a; f(ax) stretches horizontally by factor \frac1a.
Partial fractions
\frac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}

Put x=1: 6=3A, so A=2. Put x=-2: -9=-3B, so B=3.

  • For a repeated factor (x-a)^2 use \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^2}.
Exam tips

For "show that" questions, every step must be visible. Don't jump straight to the given answer.

  • State the domain and range when asked about f^{-1}. Many marks are lost here.
m-coord:
Straight lines
  • Gradient m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}; line y-y_1=m(x-x_1).
  • Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have m_1m_2=-1.
  • Midpoint \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}2,\frac{y_1+y_2}2\right); distance \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}.
Circles
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2
  • Centre (a,b), radius r. Complete the square to convert x^2+y^2+2fx+2gy+c=0.
  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  • A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90^\circ, so a right-angled triangle's hypotenuse is a diameter.
  • Line meets circle: substitute, then use the discriminant (>0 two points, =0 tangent, <0 none).
Parametric equations
  • x=f(t), y=g(t). To get the Cartesian form, eliminate t, e.g. using \sin^2t+\cos^2t=1.
  • Example: x=3\cos t, y=3\sin t gives x^2+y^2=9.
Worked example

Find the tangent to x^2+y^2-4x+6y-12=0 at (5,1).

Centre (2,-3), so the radius gradient is \frac{1-(-3)}{5-2}=\frac43. The tangent gradient is -\frac34:

y-1=-\tfrac34(x-5)\ \Rightarrow\ 3x+4y-19=0
Exam tips
  • Give the line in the form the question asks for (e.g. ax+by+c=0 with integers).
  • Watch your signs: in (x-a)^2 the centre is at +a.
m-seq:
Binomial expansion
(a+b)^n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom nr a^{n-r}b^r
  • For any rational n: (1+x)^n=1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2+\dots, valid for |x|<1.
  • For (a+bx)^n, first take out a^n: a^n\left(1+\frac bax\right)^n, valid for |x|<\left|\frac ab\right|.
Arithmetic sequences
u_n=a+(n-1)d
S_n=\tfrac n2\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]=\tfrac n2(a+l)
Geometric sequences
u_n=ar^{n-1}
S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}
S_\infty=\frac a{1-r}\ \ (|r|<1)
Other sequences
  • Recurrence u_{n+1}=f(u_n): increasing, decreasing or periodic (repeats with some order k).
  • Sigma notation: \sum_{r=1}^{n}1=n. Watch the start value.
Worked example

A geometric series has u_2=12 and S_\infty=64. Find r.

ar=12 and \frac a{1-r}=64, so 12=64r(1-r). This gives 16r^2-16r+3=0, i.e. (4r-1)(4r-3)=0, so r=\frac14 or r=\frac34.

Exam tips

Always state the validity range of a binomial expansion with a non-integer or negative n.

  • When solving S_n>k by logs, dividing by \ln r with r<1 flips the inequality.
m-trig:
Basics
  • Radians: \pi\text{ rad}=180^\circ. Arc length s=r\theta; sector area A=\frac12r^2\theta (\theta in radians).
  • Small angles: \sin\theta\approx\theta, \tan\theta\approx\theta, \cos\theta\approx1-\frac{\theta^2}2.
  • Sine rule \frac a{\sin A}=\frac b{\sin B} (watch for the ambiguous case). Cosine rule a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A. Area \frac12ab\sin C.
Identities
\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1
1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta
1+\cot^2\theta=\csc^2\theta
\sin(A\pm B)=\sin A\cos B\pm\cos A\sin B
\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B
\sin2A=2\sin A\cos A
\cos2A=1-2\sin^2A=2\cos^2A-1
\tan2A=\frac{2\tan A}{1-\tan^2A}
Harmonic form

a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=R\sin(\theta+\alpha), where R=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} and \tan\alpha=\frac ba.

  • Max value R, min value -R. Use it to solve equations and find extrema.
Inverse trig
  • \arcsin: domain [-1,1], range [-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]. \arccos: range [0,\pi]. \arctan: range (-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2).
Worked example

Solve 2\cos^2x=1+\sin x for 0\le x<2\pi.

2(1-\sin^2x)=1+\sin x \Rightarrow 2\sin^2x+\sin x-1=0 \Rightarrow (2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)=0.

So \sin x=\frac12, giving x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6; or \sin x=-1, giving x=\frac{3\pi}2.

Exam tips

Check the interval and units (degrees or radians). Find all solutions using the CAST diagram or the graph's symmetry.

  • Never divide both sides by \sin x: you lose the solutions where \sin x=0. Factorise instead.
m-exp:
Key facts
  • y=a^x passes through (0,1). y=e^x has gradient equal to its value: \frac d{dx}e^{kx}=ke^{kx}.
  • \log_a x=n \iff a^n=x; \ln x=\log_e x.
\log a+\log b=\log ab
\log a-\log b=\log\tfrac ab
k\log a=\log a^k
  • Change of base: \log_a x=\frac{\ln x}{\ln a}.
Modelling
  • Growth/decay: N=N_0e^{kt} (k>0 growth, k<0 decay).
  • Linearising: if y=ax^n then \log y=\log a+n\log x (gradient n, intercept \log a). If y=kb^x then \log y=\log k+x\log b.
Worked example

Solve 3^{2x}-4\cdot3^x+3=0.

Let u=3^x: u^2-4u+3=0, so u=1 or u=3, giving x=0 or x=1.

Exam tips

In modelling questions, interpret the constants in context (e.g. N_0 is the initial value) and comment on limitations of the model.

  • \ln(a+b)\neq\ln a+\ln b. This is a very common error.
  • e^x>0 for all x, so reject any solution that needs e^x\le0.
m-diff:
Rules
\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}
\frac{d}{dx}e^{kx}=ke^{kx}
\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x
\frac{d}{dx}\sin kx=k\cos kx
\frac{d}{dx}\cos kx=-k\sin kx
\frac{d}{dx}\tan kx=k\sec^2kx
  • Chain rule: \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}. Product rule: (uv)'=u'v+uv'. Quotient rule: \left(\frac uv\right)'=\frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}.
  • First principles: f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.
Applications
  • Tangent gradient f'(a); normal gradient -\frac1{f'(a)}.
  • Stationary points where f'(x)=0: f''>0 minimum, f''<0 maximum.
  • Points of inflection: f''(x)=0 and f'' changes sign. Concave where f''<0, convex where f''>0.
  • Increasing where f'(x)>0.
Implicit and parametric
  • Implicit: differentiate each term w.r.t. x, so \frac d{dx}y^2=2y\frac{dy}{dx} and \frac d{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx}.
  • Parametric: \frac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}.
  • Connected rates: \frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\cdot\frac{dr}{dt}.
Worked example

y=x^2e^{3x}: \ \frac{dy}{dx}=2xe^{3x}+3x^2e^{3x}=xe^{3x}(2+3x).

Exam tips

For the nature of a stationary point you must show the f'' value (or the sign change) and state the conclusion.

  • In optimisation, check that the answer makes sense (e.g. a length must be positive).
m-int:
Standard results
\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c\ (n\neq-1)
\int\frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+c
\int e^{kx}dx=\tfrac1ke^{kx}+c
\int\cos kx\,dx=\tfrac1k\sin kx+c
\int\sin kx\,dx=-\tfrac1k\cos kx+c
  • \int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\ln|f(x)|+c, and \int\sec^2kx\,dx=\frac1k\tan kx+c.
Techniques
  • Substitution: change dx and the limits.
  • By parts: \int u\frac{dv}{dx}dx=uv-\int v\frac{du}{dx}dx. Choose u to be the factor that simplifies when differentiated (but take u=\ln x).
  • Partial fractions for rational functions.
  • Trig identities, e.g. \cos^2x=\frac12(1+\cos2x).
Areas and differential equations
  • The area between curve and x-axis is \int_a^b y\,dx. Regions below the axis give negative values, so split them up.
  • Area between curves: \int(\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dx.
  • Separable DE: \frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y) \Rightarrow \int\frac1{g(y)}dy=\int f(x)\,dx. Use the initial conditions to find c.
  • Trapezium rule: \int_a^b y\,dx\approx\frac h2\left[y_0+2(y_1+\dots+y_{n-1})+y_n\right], where h=\frac{b-a}n.
Worked example

\displaystyle\int_1^e x\ln x\,dx: take u=\ln x, v'=x. Then

\left[\tfrac{x^2}2\ln x\right]_1^e-\int_1^e\tfrac x2\,dx=\tfrac{e^2}2-\tfrac{e^2-1}4=\tfrac{e^2+1}4
Exam tips

Don't forget +c on indefinite integrals, and the modulus in \ln|x|.

  • Trapezium rule: an overestimate if the curve is convex, an underestimate if concave.
m-num:
Locating roots
  • If f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in (a,b).
  • It can fail if f has an asymptote in the interval, or if there are two roots close together.
Iteration
  • Rearrange f(x)=0 to x=g(x) and iterate x_{n+1}=g(x_n).
  • It converges if |g'(x)|<1 near the root. Staircase diagram if g'>0, cobweb if g'<0.
Newton–Raphson
x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}
  • It fails if f'(x_n)\approx0 (tangent nearly horizontal), or if the start value is far from the root.
Worked example

f(x)=x^3-2x-5, x_0=2: f(2)=-1 and f'(2)=10, so x_1=2.1.

To show a root is 2.09 to 2 d.p., check that f(2.085) and f(2.095) have opposite signs.

Exam tips

To justify accuracy, use the sign change on the bounds (\pm0.005 for 2 d.p.), then conclude in words.
m-vec:
Basics
  • \mathbf a=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j+z\mathbf k; magnitude |\mathbf a|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}; unit vector \frac{\mathbf a}{|\mathbf a|}.
  • \overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other.
  • Position vector of a point dividing AB in the ratio m:n: \mathbf a+\frac m{m+n}(\mathbf b-\mathbf a).
  • Direction angle with the x-axis: \cos\theta_x=\frac x{|\mathbf a|}.
Geometry
  • Collinear points: show \overrightarrow{AB}=k\overrightarrow{BC} and that they share a point.
  • In 2D, a vector at bearing/angle \theta to \mathbf i with magnitude r is r\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+r\sin\theta\,\mathbf j.
Worked example

A(1,2,3) and B(4,6,3): \overrightarrow{AB}=3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j, so |AB|=5 and the unit vector is \frac15(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j).

Exam tips

Show vector working clearly in column or \mathbf{ijk} form. In proofs, state the conclusion (e.g. "hence ABCD is a parallelogram").
s-samp:
Key terms
  • Population: the whole group. Census: observe every member. Sample: a subset.
  • Sampling frame: a list of the members of the population.
Methods
  • Simple random: every sample of size n is equally likely (random numbers or lottery).
  • Systematic: every k-th item from a list, with a random start; k=\frac Nn.
  • Stratified: sample from each stratum in proportion to its size, e.g. \frac{80}{200}\times30=12.
  • Quota: the interviewer fills quotas for each group. Non-random, so it may be biased, but no frame is needed.
  • Opportunity: whoever is available. Easy, but unlikely to be representative.
Large data set
  • Know the Edexcel LDS: weather data from UK and overseas stations, 1987 and 2015. "tr" means trace (under 0.05 mm of rain). Look out for n/a values.
Exam tips

When criticising a method, refer to the context (e.g. "only people at the gym at 9 am are sampled, so it is not representative").

  • Stratified and quota sampling both use groups. Stratified is random within each group; quota is not.
s-data:
Measures
\bar x=\frac{\sum x}n
\sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}n-\bar x^2=\frac{S_{xx}}n
  • Median and quartiles for grouped data come from interpolation. IQR =Q_3-Q_1.
  • Coding y=\frac{x-a}b: \bar y=\frac{\bar x-a}b and \sigma_y=\frac{\sigma_x}b.
Diagrams
  • Histogram: frequency density =\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}; area is proportional to frequency.
  • Box plots: outliers are usually below Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR} or above Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}.
  • Cumulative frequency: plot at the upper class boundaries.
Correlation and regression
  • PMCC r lies between -1 and 1. Correlation does not imply causation.
  • Regression line y=a+bx: interpret b as the change in y per unit of x. Only predict within the data range (interpolation).
Exam tips

When comparing distributions, compare a location (median or mean) and a spread (IQR or s.d.), both in context.

  • Use the median and IQR when there are outliers or skew.
s-prob:
Rules
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A\cap B)=0. Independent: P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
  • Independence also means P(A\mid B)=P(A).
Tools
  • Venn diagrams: fill from the centre outwards.
  • Tree diagrams: multiply along branches and add between outcomes. The second-stage branches are conditional.
  • Two-way tables.
Worked example

P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A\cup B)=0.7. Then P(A\cap B)=0.2=0.4\times0.5, so A and B are independent.

P(A\mid B)=\frac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4.

Worked example 2 (tree diagram)

A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(\text{second red}\mid\text{first blue}) and P(\text{both same colour}).

  • P(R_2\mid B_1)=\frac34.
  • P(\text{same})=\frac35\cdot\frac24+\frac25\cdot\frac14=\frac{6}{20}+\frac{2}{20}=\frac25.
  • Without replacement, the second-stage probabilities change, so the events are not independent.
Exam tips

To prove independence, show a numerical equality such as P(A\cap B)=P(A)\times P(B) and state the conclusion.
s-dist:
Binomial X\sim B(n,p)
  • Conditions: fixed n; independent trials; two outcomes; constant p.
P(X=r)=\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}
  • Use cumulative tables or a calculator: P(X\ge r)=1-P(X\le r-1).
Normal X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)
  • Symmetric bell curve. About 68% of values lie within 1\sigma, 95% within 2\sigma, and 99.7% within 3\sigma. The points of inflection are at \mu\pm\sigma.
  • Standardise: Z=\frac{X-\mu}\sigma\sim N(0,1).
  • Normal approximation to B(n,p) when n is large and p\approx0.5: \mu=np, \sigma^2=np(1-p). Use a continuity correction, e.g. P(X\le 10)\to P(Y<10.5).
Worked example

X\sim N(50,4^2) with P(X>a)=0.1: \frac{a-50}{4}=1.2816, so a=55.1.

Exam tips

Remember the variance is \sigma^2: N(50,16) means \sigma=4.

  • Discrete distribution: probabilities sum to 1.
s-hyp:
Method

1. State H_0 and H_1 in terms of the parameter (p, \mu or \rho).

2. Choose the significance level (e.g. 5%). For a two-tailed test, put 2.5\% in each tail.

3. Under H_0, find the probability of the observed value or more extreme (or find the critical region).

4. Compare, then conclude in context.

Binomial test
  • H_0: p=0.3, H_1: p>0.3. With X\sim B(20,0.3), test P(X\ge x_{\text{obs}}).
  • Critical region: the set of values that leads to rejecting H_0. The actual significance level is P(\text{in CR}\mid H_0).
Normal mean
\bar X\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}n\right)
Z=\frac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
Correlation
  • H_0:\rho=0, H_1:\rho>0 (or <0, or \neq0). Compare r with the critical value from the table.
Exam tips

Write the conclusion with no certainty words: "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest that the proportion has increased."
k-units:
SI units
  • Base units: m (length), kg (mass), s (time). Derived: N = kg m s⁻², J = N m, W = J s⁻¹.
  • Convert carefully: 1\text{ km h}^{-1}=\frac{1000}{3600}\text{ m s}^{-1}.
Modelling assumptions
  • Particle: mass at one point; ignore size and rotation.
  • Rod: rigid, has length but no thickness. Lamina: flat.
  • Light: massless. Inextensible: constant length, so connected objects have equal acceleration.
  • Smooth: no friction. Rough: friction acts.
  • g=9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} unless stated. Give answers to 2–3 s.f. when g=9.8 is used.
Exam tips

When a question asks you to "state an assumption", link it to the effect it has, e.g. "treat the ball as a particle, so air resistance is ignored".
k-kin:
Constant acceleration (suvat)
v=u+at
s=ut+\tfrac12at^2
s=\tfrac12(u+v)t
v^2=u^2+2as
s=vt-\tfrac12at^2
  • Vector form: \mathbf v=\mathbf u+\mathbf at, \mathbf r=\mathbf ut+\frac12\mathbf at^2.
Graphs
  • v–t graph: gradient is acceleration; area is displacement.
Variable acceleration
v=\frac{ds}{dt}
a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2s}{dt^2}
s=\int v\,dt
v=\int a\,dt
Projectiles
  • Horizontal: u\cos\theta is constant. Vertical: u\sin\theta, with a=-g.
  • Time of flight (to the same level): \frac{2u\sin\theta}g. Max height: \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}.
Worked example

A ball is thrown at 20\text{ m s}^{-1} and 30^\circ above the horizontal. Vertical u_y=10, so it is at the top at t=\frac{10}{9.8}=1.02\text{ s}. The range on level ground is 20\cos30^\circ\times2.04=35.3\text{ m}.

Exam tips

Choose and state a positive direction. Most suvat sign errors come from mixing directions.
k-force:
Newton's laws
  • N1: constant velocity unless a resultant force acts. N2: F=ma. N3: equal and opposite forces on different bodies.
  • Weight W=mg. On a slope at angle \alpha: mg\sin\alpha down the slope, mg\cos\alpha into the slope.
Friction
F\le\mu R
  • Limiting equilibrium or moving: F=\mu R. Friction opposes the motion (or the tendency to move).
Connected particles
  • Over a smooth pulley: same tension on both sides of a light string; same acceleration if the string is inextensible.
  • Write F=ma for each particle separately (or for the whole system if moving together).
Worked example

A 3 kg block on a rough horizontal table (\mu=0.2) is pulled by a string over a pulley to a hanging 2 kg mass.

For the 2 kg mass: 2g-T=2a. For the block: T-0.2(3g)=3a. Adding gives 2g-0.6g=5a, so a=2.74\text{ m s}^{-2} and T=14.1\text{ N}.

Exam tips

Draw a large force diagram for every body. Resolve parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
k-mom:
Moments
\text{moment}=F\times d_\perp
  • d_\perp is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Unit: N m.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force =0 and total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment about any point.
  • Uniform rod: its weight acts at the centre.
  • "About to tilt" about a support: the reaction at the other support is 0.
  • Ladder problems: resolve vertically and horizontally, then take moments about the foot. Use F\le\mu R.
Worked example

A uniform 4 m plank of mass 20 kg rests on supports at end A and at B, 3 m from A. How far beyond B can a 50 kg person stand before the plank tips?

On the point of tipping about B, R_A=0. Taking moments about B: 20g\times1=50g\times d, so d=0.4\text{ m} beyond B (3.4 m from A).

Exam tips

Take moments about a point where an unknown force acts, which removes it from the equation.
p-1:
Planning and implementing
  • Independent variable: the one you change. Dependent variable: the one you measure. Control variables: kept constant.
  • Choose instruments with a suitable resolution, the smallest change they can show (e.g. a micrometer reads to 0.01 mm).
  • Repeat readings and take the mean, discarding anomalies. Check for zero errors.
Analysis
  • Accuracy: how close a value is to the true value. Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.
  • Random errors cause scatter; reduce them by repeating and averaging. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way (e.g. a zero error); they are not reduced by repeating.
  • Straight-line graphs: compare with y=mx+c. Take the gradient from a large triangle.
  • Log graphs: if y=kx^n, then \lg y=n\lg x+\lg k, so the gradient is n.
Evaluation
  • Percentage difference from the accepted value: \frac{|\text{exp}-\text{accepted}|}{\text{accepted}}\times100\%.
  • Error bars show the uncertainty. Worst-fit lines give the uncertainty in the gradient.
Exam tips

"Suggest an improvement": be specific, e.g. "use a data-logger with a light gate to remove human reaction time", not just "be more accurate".
p-2-1:
SI base units
  • kg, m, s, A, K, mol (also cd). Every other unit is derived from these, e.g. N = kg m s⁻², J = kg m² s⁻², V = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹, C = A s.
Prefixes
  • p 10^{-12}, n 10^{-9}, μ 10^{-6}, m 10^{-3}, c 10^{-2}, k 10^{3}, M 10^{6}, G 10^{9}, T 10^{12}.
Homogeneity
  • An equation is homogeneous if both sides have the same base units. This is necessary for the equation to be correct, but not sufficient (numerical constants such as \frac12 can't be checked this way).
Worked example

Check that E_k=\frac12mv^2 is homogeneous: \text{kg}\,(\text{m s}^{-1})^2=\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-2}=\text{J} ✓.

Estimation
  • Mass of an adult ≈ 70 kg; walking speed ≈ 1.5 m s⁻¹; height of a room ≈ 2.5 m; power of a kettle ≈ 2 kW.
Exam tips

Convert everything to base SI units before substituting into equations. Squared prefixes trip people up: 1\text{ cm}^2=10^{-4}\text{ m}^2.
p-2-2:
Uncertainties
  • Absolute uncertainty: e.g. (2.40\pm0.05)\text{ m}. Percentage uncertainty =\frac{\Delta x}{x}\times100\%.
  • Adding or subtracting quantities: add the absolute uncertainties.
  • Multiplying or dividing: add the percentage uncertainties.
  • Powers: y=x^n gives (% in y) = n\times(% in x).
  • Uncertainty from repeat readings: \pm\frac12\timesrange.
  • From a graph: \%\text{ uncertainty}=\frac{|\text{best}-\text{worst gradient}|}{\text{best gradient}}\times100\%.
Worked example

Diameter d=(0.50\pm0.01) mm is a 2% uncertainty, so the area A=\frac{\pi d^2}{4} has uncertainty 2\times2\%=4\%.

Resistivity \rho=\frac{RA}{L} with R ±3% and L ±1%: the total is 3+4+1=8\%.

Significant figures
  • Give the final answer to the same number of s.f. as the least precise data.
  • The uncertainty in a mean is about half the range of the repeat readings. Anomalies are excluded before averaging.
Exam tips

Quote the final uncertainty to 1 (or 2) significant figures, and match the decimal places of the value to it.
p-2-3:
Scalars and vectors
  • Scalar: magnitude only (mass, speed, energy, distance). Vector: magnitude and direction (force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum).
Combining vectors
  • Two perpendicular vectors: R=\sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2}, at angle \theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{F_2}{F_1}.
  • Non-perpendicular: use a scale drawing, or the cosine rule (R^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C).
  • Equilibrium of three coplanar forces: they form a closed triangle.
Resolving
F_x=F\cos\theta,\qquad F_y=F\sin\theta
  • On a slope at \theta: the component of weight along the slope is mg\sin\theta; perpendicular to it is mg\cos\theta.
Worked example

A 12 N force acts at 30^\circ above the horizontal: F_x=12\cos30^\circ=10.4 N and F_y=6.0 N.

Exam tips

Make sure the angle you use is the one between the force and the direction you are resolving along.
p-3-1:
Definitions
  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction. Velocity v=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}. Acceleration a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}.
  • Graphs: the gradient of s–t is velocity; the gradient of v–t is acceleration; the area under v–t is displacement.
suvat (constant acceleration)
v=u+at
s=\tfrac12(u+v)t
s=ut+\tfrac12at^2
v^2=u^2+2as
Free fall and projectiles
  • Free fall: g=9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}. Measure g with light gates, a trapdoor and electromagnet, or video.
  • Projectiles: horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Horizontal velocity is constant (no air resistance); vertical acceleration is g.
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance (v\times reaction time) + braking distance.
Worked example

A ball is kicked horizontally at 8.0\text{ m s}^{-1} off a 20 m cliff. Vertically: 20=\frac12(9.81)t^2, so t=2.02 s. Horizontal distance: 8.0\times2.02=16 m.

Exam tips

List your s, u, v, a, t values first, and take one direction as positive (e.g. up = +, so a=-9.81).

  • Doubling the speed doubles the thinking distance but quadruples the braking distance.
p-3-2:
Forces
  • F=ma; weight W=mg. Drag increases with speed. Terminal velocity is reached when drag + upthrust = weight, so a=0.
  • Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced =\rho Vg (Archimedes).
  • Pressure p=\frac FA. In a fluid, p=h\rho g.
Moments and equilibrium
  • Moment =F\times d_\perp. Couple: torque =F\times perpendicular separation of the two forces.
  • Principle of moments: in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments, and the resultant force is zero.
  • Centre of mass: the point where the weight appears to act.
Worked example

A 500 g object is fully submerged in water (\rho=1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}) with volume 2.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^3. Upthrust =1000\times2.0\times10^{-4}\times9.81=1.96 N, so its apparent weight is 4.91-1.96=2.95 N.

Exam tips

Free-body diagrams: label every force, and draw each arrow from the point where the force acts.
p-3-3:
Work and energy
W=Fx\cos\theta
  • 1 J is the work done when a 1 N force moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.
  • E_k=\frac12mv^2; \Delta E_p=mg\Delta h.
  • Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. E.g. a falling object has v=\sqrt{2gh} (no drag).
Power and efficiency
P=\frac{W}{t}=Fv
\text{efficiency}=\frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\times100\%
Worked example

A car with a 30 kW engine has a top speed of 25\text{ m s}^{-1}. The resistive force is F=\frac Pv=\frac{30000}{25}=1200 N.

Exam tips

Work is done only by the force component along the displacement. A force at right angles to the motion does no work (e.g. the centripetal force).
p-3-4:
Springs
  • Hooke's law: F=kx (up to the limit of proportionality).
  • Elastic potential energy E=\frac12Fx=\frac12kx^2, the area under the F–x graph.
  • Series springs: \frac1k=\frac1{k_1}+\frac1{k_2}. Parallel springs: k=k_1+k_2.
Materials
\sigma=\frac FA,\qquad \varepsilon=\frac xL,\qquad E=\frac\sigma\varepsilon
  • Young modulus unit: Pa. Find it from the gradient of the linear part of the stress–strain graph.
  • Elastic deformation: returns to its original shape. Plastic: permanent extension.
  • Ductile (copper): large plastic region. Brittle (glass): breaks with no plastic deformation. Polymeric (rubber): loading and unloading curves differ (hysteresis); the area between them is energy lost as heat.
  • UTS: the maximum stress a material can withstand.
Exam tips

Determining E for a wire: use a long wire (larger extension), measure the diameter with a micrometer in several places, and use the gradient of the stress–strain graph.
p-3-5:
Newton's laws
  • N1: a body stays at rest or at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
  • N2: F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}, which gives F=ma for constant mass.
  • N3: when A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A.
Momentum
p=mv,\qquad \text{impulse}=F\Delta t=\Delta p
  • Impulse is the area under the F–t graph (unit N s).
  • Momentum is conserved in a closed system.
  • Elastic collision: kinetic energy is also conserved. Inelastic collision: some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms.
Worked example

A 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1} hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together: 6.0=3.0v, so v=2.0\text{ m s}^{-1}. Kinetic energy goes from 9.0 J to 6.0 J, so the collision is inelastic.

Exam tips

Momentum is a vector, so give a sign to each direction. Airbags and crumple zones increase \Delta t, which reduces the force for the same \Delta p.
p-4-1:
Charge and current
I=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}
  • 1 C is the charge passing a point when 1 A flows for 1 s. Elementary charge e=1.60\times10^{-19} C, so charge is quantised.
  • Kirchhoff's 1st law: the current into a junction equals the current out (conservation of charge).
  • In metals, the charge carriers are electrons. In electrolytes, they are ions.
Mean drift velocity
I=Anev
  • n is the number density of charge carriers. Metals have n\approx10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}, so v is tiny (about mm s⁻¹). Semiconductors have a much smaller n.
Worked example

I=2.0 A in copper (n=8.5\times10^{28}) with A=1.0\times10^{-6}\text{ m}^2: v=\frac{2.0}{1.0\times10^{-6}\times8.5\times10^{28}\times1.6\times10^{-19}}=1.5\times10^{-4}\text{ m s}^{-1}.

Exam tips

If a wire narrows, the current is the same, so a smaller A means the drift velocity increases.
p-4-2:
Definitions
  • p.d. V=\frac WQ: energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge. e.m.f. \varepsilon=\frac WQ: energy transferred to electrical form per unit charge.
  • Energy gained by an electron accelerated through V: eV=\frac12mv^2.
  • Resistance R=\frac VI. Ohm's law: I\propto V for a metallic conductor at constant temperature.
I–V characteristics
  • Resistor: a straight line through the origin. Filament lamp: a curve (resistance rises as it gets hotter). Diode: conducts only in forward bias, above about 0.6 V. LED: about 2 V.
  • NTC thermistor: resistance falls as temperature rises. LDR: resistance falls as light intensity rises.
Resistivity and power
R=\frac{\rho L}{A}
P=VI=I^2R=\frac{V^2}{R},\qquad W=VIt
  • 1 kWh =3.6\times10^6 J. Cost = kWh × price per kWh.
Exam tips

Resistivity is a property of the material; resistance depends on its dimensions too. For a metal, \rho rises with temperature.
p-4-3:
Circuit rules
  • Kirchhoff's 2nd law: around any loop, the sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of p.d.s (conservation of energy).
  • Series: R=R_1+R_2+\dots Parallel: \frac1R=\frac1{R_1}+\frac1{R_2}+\dots
Internal resistance
\varepsilon=I(R+r),\qquad V=\varepsilon-Ir
  • "Lost volts" =Ir. A graph of V against I has gradient -r and y-intercept \varepsilon.
Potential divider
V_{out}=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V_{in}
  • With an LDR or thermistor in place of R_2, V_{out} responds to light or temperature (sensor circuits).
  • A potentiometer gives a continuously variable output.
Worked example

\varepsilon=6.0 V, r=0.50\ \Omega, R=5.5\ \Omega: I=\frac{6.0}{6.0}=1.0 A, so the terminal p.d. is V=5.5 V.

Exam tips

An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. In potential-divider questions, say what happens to R, then to V_{out}, and why.
p-4-4:
Wave basics
v=f\lambda,\qquad f=\frac1T
  • Progressive waves transfer energy. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to it.
  • Phase difference =\frac{x}{\lambda}\times360^\circ. Intensity I=\frac PA, and I\propto A^2.
  • Only transverse waves can be polarised: their oscillations are restricted to one plane. Crossed polarising filters (or a metal grille for microwaves) block the wave.
Electromagnetic waves
  • All travel at c=3.00\times10^8\text{ m s}^{-1} in a vacuum. Order: radio, micro, IR, visible (400–700 nm), UV, X-ray, γ.
  • Refraction: n=\frac cv; n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2. Total internal reflection when \theta>C, where \sin C=\frac1n (going into air).
Superposition and stationary waves
  • Coherent sources: constant phase difference. Path difference n\lambda gives constructive interference; (n+\frac12)\lambda gives destructive.
  • Young's double slit: \lambda=\frac{ax}{D}. Grating: d\sin\theta=n\lambda.
  • Stationary waves form from two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions. Node-to-node distance =\frac\lambda2. They store energy rather than transferring it.
  • Pipe closed at one end: L=\frac\lambda4 for the fundamental. String or open pipe: L=\frac\lambda2.
Exam tips

In Young's slits, a is the slit separation, x is the fringe spacing, and D is the slit-to-screen distance. Measure across several fringes and divide.
p-4-5:
Photons
E=hf=\frac{hc}{\lambda}
  • 1 eV =1.60\times10^{-19} J. LEDs can be used to find h: eV_0=\frac{hc}\lambda.
Photoelectric effect
hf=\phi+KE_{max}
  • The threshold frequency is f_0=\frac\phi h. Below it, no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
  • A higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons, but not a higher KE_{max}.
  • Emission is instantaneous and one-to-one (one photon, one electron). This is evidence for the particle nature of light.
Wave–particle duality
\lambda=\frac hp=\frac h{mv}
  • Electron diffraction through graphite is evidence that particles behave as waves (spacing ≈ λ).
Worked example

UV of wavelength 200 nm falls on a metal with \phi=4.5 eV. E=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.0\times10^8}{200\times10^{-9}}=9.9\times10^{-19}\text{ J}=6.2 eV, so KE_{max}=1.7 eV.

Exam tips

Convert between eV and J carefully. Wave theory can't explain the threshold frequency; only the photon model can.
p-5-1:
Temperature and phases
  • Thermal equilibrium: no net flow of energy between objects. T(\text{K})=\theta(^\circ\text{C})+273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible internal energy.
  • Internal energy: the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the particles.
  • During a change of phase, T stays constant: the potential energy changes, not the kinetic energy.
Specific heat and latent heat
Q=mc\Delta\theta,\qquad Q=mL
  • c in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; L_f for fusion and L_v for vaporisation, in J kg⁻¹.
Ideal gases
pV=nRT=NkT
  • Assumptions: a large number of identical molecules moving randomly; negligible molecular volume; elastic collisions; no forces between molecules except during collisions; collision time much less than the time between collisions.
pV=\tfrac13Nm\overline{c^2},\qquad \tfrac12m\overline{c^2}=\tfrac32kT
  • k=\frac R{N_A}=1.38\times10^{-23}\text{ J K}^{-1}. The r.m.s. speed is \sqrt{\overline{c^2}}.
  • Boyle's law: pV is constant at constant T.
Worked example

Mean KE of a molecule at 300 K: \frac32\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300=6.2\times10^{-21} J.

Exam tips

Always use kelvin in gas equations. n is in moles; N is the number of molecules.
p-5-2:
Circular motion
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f,\qquad v=\omega r
a=\frac{v^2}r=\omega^2r,\qquad F=\frac{mv^2}r=m\omega^2r
  • 1 radian is the angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius.
  • Constant speed but changing velocity, so it is accelerating towards the centre. The centripetal force is provided by something real (tension, gravity, friction, a reaction force).
Vertical circles
  • At the top: T+mg=\frac{mv^2}r. At the bottom: T-mg=\frac{mv^2}r.
  • Minimum speed at the top (string just slack): v=\sqrt{gr}.
Worked example

A 0.20 kg mass on a 0.50 m string moves at 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1} in a horizontal circle (on a table): F=\frac{0.20\times9.0}{0.50}=3.6 N.

Exam tips

Centripetal force is not an extra force on the free-body diagram. It is the resultant of the real forces.
p-5-3:
SHM
a=-\omega^2x
  • SHM: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.
x=A\cos\omega t
v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2},\qquad v_{max}=\omega A
  • The period is independent of amplitude (isochronous). Pendulum: T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac Lg}. Mass–spring: T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac mk}.
  • Energy swaps between KE and PE; the total is constant (\propto A^2) without damping.
Damping and resonance
  • Light damping: the amplitude decays gradually. Critical damping: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping: returns slowly.
  • Forced oscillations: resonance happens when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude. Damping lowers and broadens the peak (and shifts it slightly lower).
Worked example

A=0.050 m, f=2.0 Hz: \omega=4\pi, so v_{max}=0.63\text{ m s}^{-1} and a_{max}=\omega^2A=7.9\text{ m s}^{-2}.

Exam tips

Use x=A\sin\omega t if timing starts at equilibrium, and \cos if it starts at maximum displacement. Set your calculator to radians.
p-5-4:
Fields
g=\frac Fm,\qquad g=-\frac{GM}{r^2}
  • Field lines are radial for a point mass and uniform close to the Earth's surface. G=6.67\times10^{-11}\text{ N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}.
  • Newton's law: F=-\frac{GMm}{r^2}, which is attractive.
Orbits
  • Kepler 1: elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus. Kepler 2: equal areas in equal times. Kepler 3: T^2\propto r^3.
T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3,\qquad v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}r}
  • Geostationary orbit: T=24 h, above the equator, moving in the same direction as the Earth spins.
Potential
V_g=-\frac{GM}r,\qquad E=-\frac{GMm}r
  • Potential is the work done per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity to that point. It is negative.
  • Escape velocity: v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}r}.
  • The area under a force–distance graph is the work done (change in potential energy).
Exam tips

r is measured from the centre of the planet, so add the planet's radius to the height of the orbit.
p-5-5:
Stars
  • Life cycle: nebula, protostar, main sequence (H fusion). Low-mass stars become red giants, then white dwarfs. High-mass stars become red supergiants, then a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole.
  • Chandrasekhar limit: 1.44M_\odot; electron degeneracy pressure supports a white dwarf below it.
  • HR diagram: luminosity against temperature (temperature *decreasing* to the right).
Radiation
\lambda_{max}T=\text{constant}\ (2.9\times10^{-3}\text{ m K})
L=4\pi r^2\sigma T^4
  • Energy levels: \Delta E=hf. Emission and absorption line spectra. Grating: d\sin\theta=n\lambda.
Cosmology
  • Units: 1 AU (Earth–Sun distance), 1 ly, 1 pc ≈ 3.1\times10^{16} m. Parallax: p(\text{arcsec})=\frac1{d(\text{pc})}.
  • Doppler: \frac{\Delta\lambda}\lambda\approx\frac vc. Hubble's law v=H_0d; the age of the universe is about \frac1{H_0}.
  • Cosmological principle: the universe is isotropic and homogeneous on large scales. Evidence for the Big Bang: the CMB (about 2.7 K) and galactic redshift. Dark matter and dark energy.
Exam tips

Convert H_0 from km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ to s⁻¹ before computing the age: 1\text{ Mpc}=3.1\times10^{22} m.
p-6-1:
Capacitance
C=\frac QV,\qquad W=\tfrac12QV=\tfrac12CV^2=\frac{Q^2}{2C}
  • Series: \frac1C=\frac1{C_1}+\frac1{C_2}. Parallel: C=C_1+C_2.
  • Parallel plates: C=\frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rA}d.
Charging and discharging
\tau=RC
x=x_0e^{-t/RC}\ \text{(discharge: } Q,V,I\text{)}
V=V_0\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)\ \text{(charging)}
  • After t=RC, the value falls to 37% (discharge).
  • The \ln V–t graph for a discharge is a straight line with gradient -\frac1{RC}.
  • The area under an I–t graph is the charge. The area under a V–Q graph is the energy.
Worked example

C=470\ \muF and R=10 kΩ give \tau=4.7 s. The time to fall to half voltage is t=RC\ln2=3.3 s.

Exam tips

The current reverses direction on discharge, but in both charging and discharging it decays exponentially.
p-6-2:
Electric fields
E=\frac Fq,\qquad F=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2},\qquad E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}
  • Uniform field between parallel plates: E=\frac Vd. Field lines run from + to −.
  • A charged particle entering at right angles to a uniform field follows a parabolic path (like a projectile).
Potential
V=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r},\qquad E_p=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}
  • Equipotentials are perpendicular to the field lines. E=-\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}.
  • Capacitance of an isolated sphere: C=4\pi\varepsilon_0R.
Comparison with gravity
  • Both are inverse-square laws. Gravity is always attractive; electric forces can attract or repel.
Exam tips

\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}. Keep signs on charges when calculating potential, but use magnitudes for the size of a force and state its direction.
p-6-3:
Magnetic forces
F=BIL\sin\theta,\qquad F=BQv
  • Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion.
  • 1 T is the field that exerts 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field.
  • A charged particle in a field moves in a circle: r=\frac{mv}{BQ}. Velocity selector: v=\frac EB.
Electromagnetic induction
\phi=BA\cos\theta,\qquad \varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta(N\phi)}{\Delta t}
  • Faraday: the induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage. Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that caused it.
  • Transformers: \frac{n_s}{n_p}=\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{I_p}{I_s} (if 100% efficient).
Exam tips

Flux linkage N\phi has units Wb (or Wb-turns). Step-up transformers increase V and reduce I for transmission, giving smaller I^2R losses.
p-6-4:
The nucleus
  • Rutherford α-scattering: most pass straight through (atom mostly empty space); a few are deflected through large angles (small, dense, positive nucleus).
  • Radius R=r_0A^{1/3} with r_0\approx1.2 fm. Nuclear density is constant (about 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}).
  • Strong nuclear force: attractive up to about 3 fm, repulsive below about 0.5 fm.
Particles
  • Hadrons (baryons qqq, mesons q q̄) feel the strong force; leptons (e, μ, ν) do not.
  • Quarks: u +\frac23e, d -\frac13e, s -\frac13e. Proton uud, neutron udd.
  • β⁻ decay: d\to u+e^-+\bar\nu_e. β⁺ decay: u\to d+e^++\nu_e (weak interaction).
Radioactivity
A=\lambda N,\qquad N=N_0e^{-\lambda t},\qquad \lambda t_{1/2}=\ln2
  • α: 2p2n, highly ionising, stopped by paper. β: stopped by a few mm of aluminium. γ: reduced by lead.
Binding energy
\Delta E=\Delta mc^2
  • Mass defect: the mass of the separated nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy per nucleon peaks at Fe-56. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both release energy.
  • 1 u =931.5 MeV.
Exam tips

Fission reactors: the moderator slows neutrons (elastic collisions), control rods absorb neutrons, and the coolant removes heat.
p-6-5:
X-rays
  • Produced when fast electrons hit a tungsten target (about 1% efficiency). Attenuation: I=I_0e^{-\mu x}.
  • Mechanisms: simple scatter (1–20 keV), photoelectric effect (< 100 keV), Compton scattering (0.5–5 MeV), pair production (> 1.02 MeV).
  • Contrast media (barium, iodine) have a high atomic number Z, so they absorb strongly. CAT scans build a 3D image from slices taken by a rotating X-ray tube.
Nuclear medicine
  • Tracers such as technetium-99m (γ emitter, 6 h half-life). Gamma camera: collimator, scintillator, photomultiplier tubes.
  • PET: a β⁺ tracer (e.g. F-18 in FDG). Annihilation produces two 511 keV γ photons in opposite directions.
Ultrasound
  • Above 20 kHz, produced with the piezoelectric effect. A-scan and B-scan. Doppler for blood flow: \Delta f=\frac{2fv\cos\theta}c.
  • Acoustic impedance Z=\rho c. Reflected fraction: \frac{I_r}{I_0}=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2}{(Z_2+Z_1)^2}. Gel is used to match impedance, because air–skin reflects almost everything.
Exam tips

Compare techniques by resolution, ionising risk, cost and what they image (bone/soft tissue/function).
